title: Agents design their own governance process, but only inside an eight-element template the Atlas mandates
content:
A.2.2.6.2.2.2 says "the details of this process may be specified by the Agent," then subjects that freedom to four structural conditions and requires the process definition to "include the elements included in the documents herein." A.2.2.6.2.2.2.1 through .8 enumerate them: proposal format, actors eligible to submit proposals, requirements for a proposal to be included in a vote, voting period, quorum requirement, approval threshold, handling of emergency or urgent situations, and any special voting processes such as supermajority subject matter.

The pattern is **mandatory fields, free values**. The Atlas does not tell an Agent what its quorum should be; it forbids an Agent from not having one. Every Agent's governance is therefore comparable field-by-field, and no Agent can leave a governance question implicit and resolve it opportunistically later.

That second effect is the substantive one. Requiring emergency procedures and special voting processes to be pre-declared removes the most common governance failure mode — inventing an expedited path during the crisis that makes it convenient. Consistent with the Atlas's broader stance on pre-established override methods, the escape hatch must exist before it is needed.

The scheme also gives the Operational Facilitator something concrete to review against. A.2.2.6.2.1.2.2 has the Facilitator check each proposal for compliance with the Agent's own stated requirements, which is only possible because those requirements are guaranteed to exist in a known shape.
description: Proposal format, eligible proposers, inclusion requirements, voting period, quorum, approval threshold, emergency procedures and special processes must all be specified
